quote: Thankfully, the midwives took over at around 9am this morning, which means I havent had to play emotional support, punching bag, motivational coach, decision maker and midwife all at the same time.
cx: A father nearly 48 hours into his wife's planned home birth with a hired midwife company.

quote: My dad put the photo into ChatGPT and had it edit her sleepsuit into an England shirt. I immediately asked him not to do that. To be fair, he deleted the image from the chat and from ChatGPT, but his argument was that because he pays for ChatGPT, her image was "locked down" and no one else could see it.
cx: UK mother of a baby born in May; her parents keep posting the baby's face.

quote: When I was pregnant, I told my parents we didn't want photos of our daughter's face posted online and explained why. My mum responded with, "Except when she's born so I can post a photo, and obviously in family photos too."
cx: The same rule, set during pregnancy.

quote: my mum has this attitude of, "By the time I was your age, I had three children and a business and I coped."
cx: Her mother's line; her partner's is "this is your battle."

quote: I thought this was good for bonding and was told in our antenatal class there's no such thing as spoiling a newborn with attention. […] However today at the 5 day check-in the midwife said no we should only do skin to skin when the baby is awake and otherwise leave it in the cot.
cx: A UK father in the first week, caught between the antenatal class and the visiting midwife.

quote: Then why can't they give consistent advice? Why does one midwife come and tell me that the number of poos isn't important it's the number of wees. Then another tells me the exact opposite?
cx: Same father on the midwife home visits.

quote: Yeah I've found it mental that in Scotland the midwives are given different guidelines based on health board. One health board can recommend colostrum harvesting but the neighbouring one can't. I find it wild that depending how far down the street you live can determine the advice you're given.
cx: Same father on why the advice differs.

quote: fortunately my MiL has been a champion and helping us by letting us sleep for several hours while she's done all the cooking, cleaning, and occasional nappy changes.
cx: Who is helping in the first week.

quote: I brought a zip up and a button up explicitly because of all the antenatal advice on skin to skin being vital. Which is why I'm so confused at the 180
cx: What he packed because of the antenatal class.

quote:
if you’re there for long enough to have visitors, tell them not to bring gifts to the hospital. It’s just more for you to deal with and pack later!  
\- you don’t need that expensive cordless breast pump before your milk comes in and before you have any idea what you’re doing feeding wise.
cx: A friend who helped a new mother pack up a UK postnatal ward.

quote: instead of packing one suitcase / bag, consider packing 2-3 smaller bags: one for labour/pre baby, one for post baby and a baby bag with just baby essentials.
cx: Same post, packing tips.

quote: We spent around 36 hours in a post-natal ward and hearing some of the birthing experiences of the other mums in there and what they went through just really astounded me.
cx: A UK first-time father, days after the birth.

quote: I was so nervous when we went into theatre; more nervous than my wife in fact. I really was trying to hide it as I wanted to show positivity and calmness being her birthing partner
cx: Same father on the planned surgical birth.

quote: My wife is one of those unlucky women who experience extreme nausea and fatigue while pregnant. Lately, this has meant that I am basically soloing all toddler and household related tasks.
cx: A father of a 2-year-old, baby two due early next year, both parents working.

quote: She was sick like this with our son but since he was our first, it was a lot different. She would just lay in bed or on the couch and watch TV or do whatever and I would take care of her and do whatever else I wanted with my free time. Obviously now things are different, since her being incapacitated means it's just me and the lad for most evenings.
cx: How the second pregnancy differs from the first, for him.

quote: From the moment we announced the pregnancy, my in-laws said they would come to help after the baby was born. In fact, I’ve been hearing about this ever since I got married four years ago. It was always presented as a given that they would come when we had our first child.
cx: 34 weeks; living in the US with in-laws in South Asia and no family nearby.

quote: As their travel date got closer, they even asked us to send a shopping list of things to bring from India. […] We even hired a cook so my mother-in-law wouldn’t have to worry about cooking if she came.
cx: What the couple had prepared for the in-laws' stay.

quote: At this point, it’s not even about whether they come or not. It’s the uncertainty that is exhausting me. I’d rather someone tell me, “We can’t come,” so we can make other plans than keep us wondering until the very last minute.
cx: After her mother-in-law began hinting the trip may not happen.

quote: almost every friend asks, “Is someone coming from your home country to help after the baby?” Every time I’m asked, it reminds me that I don’t really know what my support system will look like.
cx: The question friends keep asking her.

quote: The nursery still isn't ready, we haven't even gotten the pediatrician yet because of both of us being busy at work, there's so much to do
cx: A first-time father at 35 weeks, worried the birth may come early.

quote: I'm doing everything I can to support her. I work full time, do the grocery shopping, cook dinner, help with the household chores, take care of whatever I can around the house, and try to make her life as easy as possible. […] I feel lonely while living in the same house as the person I love most.
cx: A father of a month-old baby whose partner has withdrawn.
